title: Simulate mark-and-sweep from GC roots

blocks.text: Mark-and-sweep in two phases, as on the page. **Mark**: starting from the GC roots, follow references and mark every object reached; **an already marked object is skipped**, which is how cycles end. **Sweep**: free every unmarked object and **clear the marks of survivors** for the next collection. So **reachability from roots decides, not reference counts**: two objects that point at each other but that no root reaches are both garbage.
Write `Heap`, a simulation over named objects:

items: `allocate(name)` adds an object (a name already used is refused with `IllegalArgumentException`); `reference(from, to)` makes `from` point to `to`.
`collect()` runs mark and sweep and returns the names it freed, in allocation order; freed objects are gone from `live()` (also in allocation order).

rows: A, B, C, D; root A; A->B, B->D
X, Y; X->Y, Y->X; no roots

cases.says: With root A, A -> B and B -> D, collect() frees the unreferenced C and keeps A, B and D, reached through B.
X -> Y and Y -> X, with no root reaching either, are both freed although each is still referenced.
Marking A -> B -> A -> ... stops at the already marked A, and nothing is freed.
After a collection keeps A and B, removing root A makes the next collection free both.

concepts: Mark-and-sweep marks everything reachable from the roots, skipping objects already marked, then frees the unmarked and clears the survivors' marks.
The JVM decides garbage by reachability from GC roots, not by reference counts, so an unreachable cycle is collected.
